questions.question: Explain how the mineral revolution and the policy of confederation led Britain to wage war on African kingdoms in the late 1870s.
questions.expected_answer: Before 1870 Britain was reluctant to pay for wars or govern new territories. Diamonds made southern Africa valuable; Britain annexed Griqualand West in 1871, and Lord Carnarvon planned a confederation uniting the colonies, Boer republics and African kingdoms under British control, sending Sir Bartle Frere as High Commissioner in 1877. Independent kingdoms were seen as obstacles: they threatened security, had bought guns at the diamond fields, held land settlers wanted, and did not need to send men to work on mines and farms. Britain annexed the bankrupt South African Republic in 1877 and inherited its conflicts with the Pedi and the Zulu. Wars followed against the Xhosa in 1877 to 1878, the Zulu in 1879 and the Pedi in 1879.

questions.question: Describe the defeat of the Xhosa and the Pedi kingdoms.
questions.expected_answer: Xhosa: after a century of frontier wars and the cattle-killing of 1856 to 1857, the Gcaleka under Sarhili still held land east of the Kei. The Ninth Frontier War began in 1877 with a Gcaleka-Mfengu clash; Cape and British forces invaded, the Ngqika under Sandile joined, Sandile was killed in 1878, Sarhili went into hiding, Gcalekaland was annexed and land given to settlers and allies, and men were forced into wage labour. Pedi: Sekhukhune's kingdom in the north-eastern Transvaal defeated the South African Republic in 1876 and a British attack in 1878 after refusing British authority; in November and December 1879 Wolseley's British force with thousands of Swazi allies stormed Tsate, Sekhukhune was captured and imprisoned in Pretoria, and the Pedi lost independence and land and were drawn into migrant labour.

questions.question: Explain the causes, main events and results of the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879, and how it is remembered differently.
questions.expected_answer: Causes: Frere saw the Zulu kingdom under Cetshwayo as the main obstacle to confederation; after a boundary commission supported the Zulu land claim against the Transvaal, Frere issued an ultimatum in December 1878 demanding the army be disbanded within thirty days, which could not be accepted. Events: Chelmsford invaded in January 1879; on 22 January about 20 000 Zulu destroyed the camp at Isandlwana, killing about 1 300 on the British side; Rorke's Drift held; the Zulu lost at Khambula and finally at Ulundi on 4 July 1879. Results: Cetshwayo captured and exiled, Zululand divided into thirteen chiefdoms leading to civil war, annexed in 1887 and given to Natal in 1897, with land opened to settlers. British accounts celebrated Rorke's Drift and spoke of bringing order; Zulu memory sees a war of resistance and Isandlwana as a symbol of courage and skill.
